articles.text: Residents urged to complete an important survey What would you do if a wildfire or earthquake happened in Piedmont? Do you have plans in place for your kids and pets? In an evacuation, how long would it take you to gather essentials and get out? And most importantly – if your answer to any of the above is no, why? Not sure how to get started? Don’t have time? Do you just feel overwhelmed by it all? I know these questions aren’t fun for most people to think about. But, as your Fire Chief, I’m asking you to take 10 minutes to share your honest answers at piedmont.ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. We’ve received just over 60 responses so far, and Piedmont Fire needs to hear from a broader cross-section of residents to confidently design and deliver effective programs that will ensure our community is prepared for whatever comes. A few trends caught my eye in the early responses. First, respondents report feeling more prepared overall than I’d expected based on the existing body of research about preparedness and my personal experience from many years working in this field. With such a small sample size, it’s difficult to assess whether Piedmont already takes preparedness to a level far above what is typical in neighboring communities or if we’re looking at a self-selecting group who loves to be prepared and loves to fill out surveys about it. Second, we aren’t getting much feedback from families with school-age children. The City and Piedmont Unified School District work closely together on response plans like offering reunification services after a disaster, and we need to know how well kids and parenting adults have learned and understand those plans. Reaching out to neighbors or other family members who may need extra support in a disaster is also important for us to learn more about. Finally, I am alarmed by the low level of concern we’re seeing over the potential for wildfire in Piedmont. As a designated Wildland Urban Interface, Piedmont faces the genuine possibility of a wildfire burning through town. The 1991 Tunnel Fire claimed over 3,000 homes in Oakland and Berkeley and only stopped at Piedmont’s doorstep because of a wind change. Since then, we’ve seen numerous fires in Northern California overrun communities much further outside of historically designated wildland fire areas than Piedmont is. Creating educational and practical wildfire responses and evacuation programs for the public is a high priority for the Fire Department, so understanding Piedmonters’ perspectives on wildfire risk is an important part of this survey. Please help us help you. Complete the survey today, then send it to five friends and neighbors to take as well. Your city thanks you. For more information, call the fire department at 420-3030. articles.text: City council needs to avoid giving developer carte blanche Piedmont’s city council will soon choose between two options for locating 63 rent-controlled apartments and 133 market-rate homes on parkland in Moraga Canyon. One option would put all 199 units in Blair Park while the other would distribute them around Coaches Field. The city will provide parkland for the rent-controlled units at essentially no cost to developers. Builders of the market rate homes will compensate the city with a negotiated fraction of the value of the parkland. The council has stated that it plans to use the compensation to enhance Coaches Field. Consultants have told the council that building around Coaches Field would provide higher compensation to the city. Parcels there have excellent views and avoid Blair Park’s impediments to constructing market rate homes. Those impediments include the costs of moving sewer lines, building high retaining walls to protect new and existing homes from landslides, and protecting new homes from subsidence of the un-engineered landfill that underlies much of Blair Park. Developers of rent-controlled apartments in Blair Park would, of course, expect the city to pay all these costs. Other characteristics of Blair Park also make it the less attractive option for market rate builders. Proposals over the last two decades to add recreational facilities in Moraga Canyon were abandoned, at least in part, because three independent traffic studies found that the volume and speed of vehicles on Moraga Avenue were so great that no westerly entrance to Blair Park could meet Caltrans safety standards for corner sight distance. The proposed 199 homes in Blair Park would generate at least 800 “turns” a day through a flow of 15,000 vehicles expected to travel, without safe sightlines, on Moraga Avenue. Experience predicts that children living in Blair Park will cross Moraga Avenue to use the enhanced playfields. Driver sightlines in either direction on Moraga Avenue are dangerously short for protecting pedestrians. Reducing this risk would require that a Blair Park neighborhood be fenced along Moraga Avenue to “funnel” pedestrians to a crosswalk at Red Rock. So, residents of Piedmont’s new neighborhood would appear isolated not only by impassable terrain, retaining walls, and funneling fences, but also by dangerous access to Moraga Avenue – their only physical connection to the remainder of the community. Given the above circumstances, why would the Council even entertain the option of building an economically marginal, demonstrably unsafe, isolated enclave in Blair Park when an economically advantageous, safe neighborhood could be built across Moraga Avenue? Advocates for the Blair Park option argue that the city must maximize the economic return to prospective builders of 63 low-income housing units. Council members have stated, for example, that the City of Piedmont should approve a project that can take advantage of an Alameda County program that would give $2.3 million to any developer who can build low-income housing in Piedmont. That project, however, must be approved by January 2025. A project in Blair Park would supposedly take less time and cost to design than one on the northern side of Moraga where the issue of how to physically accommodate the expansion of Coaches Field remains unresolved. Councilmembers’ commitment to a $2.3 million subsidy for developers has, in effect, entitled the builders of 63 low-income apartments to dictate the character of an entire neighborhood of 199 homes. Advocates for the Blair Park option will, of course, object to my characterization of the current state of affairs. They will claim that Moraga Avenue can be made safer by “traffic calming” schemes such as narrowing the roadway or adding more stop lights. But such schemes were suggested a decade ago and judged infeasible for at least two reasons. First, congestion at rush hour would make Moraga Avenue virtually inaccessible for existing and new residents of the Canyon. Second, these schemes would cause vehicles to “stack” on Route 13 at the Moraga Avenue exit during rush hours. Sightlines for easterly traveling vehicles on Route 13 are too short to allow for safe “stacking.” Those advocating for the Blair Park option will also argue that building housing on the north side of Moraga will require the city to incur the unanticipated and otherwise unnecessary cost of shrinking or moving the “corporation yard” where public safety equipment is stored, staged, and repaired. This argument defies both history and logic. Several years ago, the city had a choice between building a regional aquatics center or restoring city buildings that were either or both seismically unsafe or reaching the end of useful life. The city council chose the aquatics center. Arguments for that choice included that rebuilding essential infrastructure was premature and should, when required, trigger a bond campaign that would likely succeed because Piedmonters would understand the need to upgrade police, fire, and corporation yard facilities. Members of the current council have publicly noted that the time for such a campaign is nearing because public safety facilities will continue to degrade while demand for safety services expands to serve the more than 600 recently approved new homes. The argument that building 199 homes around Coaches Field would force the city to modernize Piedmont’s safety facilities but building those same homes in Blair Park would not is absurd. Piedmont’s approval of 600 or more new homes requires modernizing police and corporation yard facilities regardless of where those homes are built. Modern police and corporation yard facilities should be consolidated in Blair Park so that a safe, economically viable, and vital neighborhood can be built around an enhanced Coaches Field. The proposed 199 homes in Blair Park would generate at least 800 “turns” a day through a flow of 15,000 vehicles expected to travel, without safe sightlines, on Moraga Avenue. Experience predicts that children living in Blair Park will cross Moraga Avenue to use the enhanced playfields. Driver sightlines in either direction on Moraga Avenue are dangerously short for protecting pedestrians. Reducing this risk would require that a Blair Park neighborhood be fenced along Moraga Avenue to “funnel” pedestrians to a crosswalk at Red Rock. So, residents of Piedmont’s new neighborhood would appear isolated not only by impassable terrain, retaining walls, and funneling fences, but also by dangerous access to Moraga Avenue – their only physical connection to the remainder of the community. Given the above circumstances, why would the Council even entertain the option of building an economically marginal, demonstrably unsafe, isolated enclave in Blair Park when an economically advantageous, safe neighborhood could be built across Moraga Avenue? Advocates for the Blair Park option argue that the city must maximize the economic return to prospective builders of 63 low-income housing units. Council members have stated, for example, that the City of Piedmont should approve a project that can take advantage of an Alameda County program that would give $2.3 million to any developer who can build low-income housing in Piedmont. That project, however, must be approved by January 2025. A project in Blair Park would supposedly take less time and cost to design than one on the northern side of Moraga where the issue of how to physically accommodate the expansion of Coaches Field remains unresolved. Councilmembers’ commitment to a $2.3 million subsidy for developers has, in effect, entitled the builders of 63 low-income apartments to dictate the character of an entire neighborhood of 199 homes. Advocates for the Blair Park option will, of course, object to my characterization of the current state of affairs. They will claim that Moraga Avenue can be made safer by “traffic calming” schemes such as narrowing the roadway or adding more stop lights. But such schemes were suggested a decade ago and judged infeasible for at least two reasons. First, congestion at rush hour would make Moraga Avenue virtually inaccessible for existing and new residents of the Canyon. Second, these schemes would cause vehicles to “stack” on Route 13 at the Moraga Avenue exit during rush hours. Sightlines for easterly traveling vehicles on Route 13 are too short to allow for safe “stacking.” Those advocating for the Blair Park option will also argue that building housing on the north side of Moraga will require the city to incur the unanticipated and otherwise unnecessary cost of shrinking or moving the “corporation yard” where public safety equipment is stored, staged, and repaired. This argument defies both history and logic. Several years ago, the city had a choice between building a regional aquatics center or restoring city buildings that were either or both seismically unsafe or reaching the end of useful life. The city council chose the aquatics center. Arguments for that choice included that rebuilding essential infrastructure was premature and should, when required, trigger a bond campaign that would likely succeed because Piedmonters would understand the need to upgrade police, fire, and corporation yard facilities. Members of the current council have publicly noted that the time for such a campaign is nearing because public safety facilities will continue to degrade while demand for safety services expands to serve the more than 600 recently approved new homes. The argument that building 199 homes around Coaches Field would force the city to modernize Piedmont’s safety facilities but building those same homes in Blair Park would not is absurd. Piedmont’s approval of 600 or more new homes requires modernizing police and corporation yard facilities regardless of where those homes are built. Modern police and corporation yard facilities should be consolidated in Blair Park so that a safe, economically viable, and vital neighborhood can be built around an enhanced Coaches Field. Final week to help Piedmont deliver preparedness programs Residents urged to complete an important survey By Fire Chief Dave Brannigan What would you do if a wildfire or earthquake happened in Piedmont? Do you have plans in place for your kids and pets? In an evacuation, how long would it take you to gather essentials and get out? And most importantly – if your answer to any of the above is no, why? Not sure how to get started? Don’t have time? Do you just feel overwhelmed by it all? I know these questions aren’t fun for most people to think about. But, as your Fire Chief, I’m asking you to take 10 minutes to share your honest answers at piedmont.ca.gov/DisasterSurvey. We’ve received just over 60 responses so far, and Piedmont Fire needs to hear from a broader cross-section of residents to confidently design and deliver effective programs that will ensure our community is prepared for whatever comes. A few trends caught my eye in the early responses. First, respondents report feeling more prepared overall than I’d expected based on the existing body of research about preparedness and my personal experience from many years working in this field. With such a small sample size, it’s difficult to assess whether Piedmont already takes preparedness to a level far above what is typical in neighboring communities or if we’re looking at a self-selecting group who loves to be prepared and loves to fill out surveys about it. Second, we aren’t getting much feedback from families with school-age children. The City and Piedmont Unified School District work closely together on response plans like offering reunification services after a disaster, and we need to know how well kids and parenting adults have learned and understand those plans. Reaching out to neighbors or other family members who may need extra support in a disaster is also important for us to learn more about. Finally, I am alarmed by the low level of concern we’re seeing over the potential for wildfire in Piedmont. As a designated Wildland Urban Interface, Piedmont faces the genuine possibility of a wildfire burning through town. The 1991 Tunnel Fire claimed over 3,000 homes in Oakland and Berkeley and only stopped at Piedmont’s doorstep because of a wind change. Since then, we’ve seen numerous fires in Northern California overrun communities much further outside of historically designated wildland fire areas than Piedmont is. Creating educational and practical wildfire responses and evacuation programs for the public is a high priority for the Fire Department, so understanding Piedmonters’ perspectives on wildfire risk is an important part of this survey. Please help us help you. Complete the survey today, then send it to five friends and neighbors to take as well. Your city thanks you. For more information, call the fire department at 420-3030. articles.text: Scouting volunteers will be recognized at the Piedmont Council’s Annual Recognition Dinner on Thursday, April 18, at the Piedmont Community Church Guild Hall. “Our volunteers support our local youth development, and provide service to the greater community as well,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “They are guiding these youth through service projects that impact our community right now — such as Scouting for Food, creek clean ups, and more. But their impact also continue for decades, as today’s Scouts carry the ethic of service throughout their lifetime.” The Silver Beaver award – the highest honor for volunteers – will be presented to Lisa Gros, a mainstay of Troop 6 and former President of the Piedmont Council. The selection committee was chaired by Chris Lee and included many longstanding Piedmont leaders. Gros was chosen for her depth and breadth of service- she served as council president during her board tenure; has served as a dedicated assistant Scoutmaster that includes leading a trek through the boundary waters of Minnesota and Canada; and has served as a Webelos den leader to help younger Scouts make the transition to a troop. She has provided outstanding support to the Order of the Arrow (an honor society for Scouts BSA), and also volunteered with the High Adventure Crew. She has consistently demonstrated cheerful service through irksome tasks and weighty responsibilities. “Working with youth, not only your own child, is one of the most meaningful legacies you can leave,” said Gros. “It’s also Lisa Gros a great way to meet other really cool adults.” The council will also recognize many other volunteers who have served in some cases for many, many years. The dinner is open to community members and tickets are available online at www.piedmontbsa.org. For more information contact Kate Benson, Executive Director, at 547-4493. articles.text: As parents, we all want what’s best for our children – to see them grow, thrive, and reach their full potential. But what if you notice that your child is struggling with certain developmental milestones? This is where early intervention comes into play, offering support and resources to help your child overcome challenges and flourish. Early intervention has the power to make a profound difference in the lives of children and families. Early intervention refers to a range of services and support systems designed to identify and address developmental delays, and other challenges in young children from birth to age three. These services aim to provide targeted interventions that promote healthy development and enhance a child’s overall well-being. One of the key principles underlying early intervention is the concept of brain plasticity – the brain’s ability to reorganize and form new connections in response to experiences and stimuli. Research has shown that the early years of life are a critical period for brain development, and early intervention can capitalize on this plasticity to promote optimal development and learning in the first three years of childhood. Research has shown that early intervention can have powerful immediate benefits, leading to significant improvements in a child’s outcomes across various Toddlers who struggle with developmental milestones can benefit from early intervention. domains, including language and communication, social skills, cognitive development, and motor skills. Numerous studies have demonstrated that children who receive early intervention services show significant improvements in various areas of development compared to those who do not receive such services. Early intervention has also been linked to long-term benefits that extend beyond childhood. A study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA) Pediatrics found that children who received early intervention services were more likely to graduate from high school, attend college, and secure employment as adults compared to those who did not receive such services. If you have concerns about your child’s development, the first step is to reach out for help. Start by talking to your child’s pediatrician and sharing your concerns. Your pediatrician can provide guidance and referrals for further evaluation if needed. Early intervention services can be coordinated through your state or local government, or can be obtained privately. During the evaluation process, a professionals will assess your child’s development and identify any areas of concern. Be open and honest about your observations and experiences with your child

articles.text: Piedmont’s youngest vocal music students hosted Spring Concerts last week at each elementary school. The 45-minute shows featured well-rehearsed performances by students in kindergarten through third grade, The theme of this year’s concerts was “Broadway,” and for vocal music teacher Adrian Behrendt, the concerts marked a big step for the young musicians. The shows kicked off bright and early, at 8:45 a.m. giving the 5-9 year olds a chance to sing like morning doves. The kids have been working with Behrendt since January on songs taken from Broadway musicals, including “Peter Pan” and “You’re a Good Man, Charlie Brown.” “When we began learning these Broadway selections, students became aware of their role as singers, listeners, and storytellers,” explained Behrendt. “They may look cute but producing a nice sound requires many skills that have been learned along the way. Performing in concert requires a student to focus on diction, expression, and choreography, all while following the conductor’s cues. Even getting onto and singing on the risers involves some learning, patience, and practice,” said Behrendt. Havens School singers held their concert in the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on Tuesday, April 2. Beach School kids performed on Thursday, April 4, and the concert at Wildwood was on Friday, April 5. Behrendts said he feels the community appreciates the effort the students have put into their performances. “Certainly, the human voice is the most personal instrument, and when shared with others, whether sung alone or as a choir, there is something in that shared human experience we can discover and appreciate,” he said. articles.text: Charming Montclair Village is the perfect spot to take a break from the bustle of the Bay during the Montclair Village Art Walk. This sidewalk art show celebrates art in the outdoors with more than 40 artists from the Bay Area displaying their handcrafted works. Support the artists the weekend of April 20-21 from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. each day. Presented by the Montclair Village Association, this free open air art gallery offers a chance to get to know the participating artists and learn the stories behind each piece they make. Among the artisans this year’s event are: Brad Berkheimer Abstract Art Brad Berkheimer has been a full-time professional decorative painter in the Monterey and Pebble Beach areas for over 40 years, specialized in many types of faux finishes, decorative painting of home interior spaces, and custom automotive painting and graphics. He transitioned those skills and experiences to find renewed joy and inspiration in the painting of original abstract artwork on canvas. “My art is guided by the forms, textures, colors and movement I find in Nature,” says Brad. “I look to create unique organic images that attempt to mimic a full spectrum of tones, dynamics and harmonic corrosion found in the natural world.” David Bowman Metal Art Consisting of David Mills Bowman and his son, Reed Christopher Bowman, David M Bowman Studio produces a range of functional and decorative metal artwork. These talented artists collaborate on the design and creation of a wide range of pieces including wall art, vases and candle holders. They construct all of the pieces by hand, with hand tools and simple machines. All the work is produced from brass and copper sheet and rod, formed into shape with shears, hammers, sanders and grinders, and brazed together using an oxyacetylene welding torch. The two do not cast work or use cast parts and they mix patina chemicals from scratch and apply them by hand. Jacque Price Paintings Jacque Price paints in oil using brush and knife, and she often incorporates oil sticks to create meandering lines that silhouette forms or ridge lines. Her process of toning the canvas in a myriad of colors when she first starts a painting sets the groundwork for creating a workable composition that then leads to inspired contextual forms in the final layers. Jacque’s current body of work is curious in nature - amorphous shapes encompass figures in contemplation, ambiguous compositions disperse focus, emotion and stillness meet along lines of vivid color. Her work reveals skill in rendering, an understanding of design, and a proclivity for nature and its influence on the human experience. Doug Rubenstein Ceramics Doug Rubenstein is a potter who uses clay as his primary medium. His work spans a range of creations and sizes. On the small side, he sells dishes, jewelry holders, salt cellars, breakfast bowls, mugs, and tumblers. The medium items include ramen bowls, side plates, dinner plates, jars and pasta bowls. Larger items are vases and serving bowls. “I like to think of my artwork as part of a fifth season - or a season of feeling - honoring, digesting and fathoming that which the world unfolds for us each year,” says Doug. “I design with aesthetics and textures that respect, pay homage and connect to nature while exploring the marriage between natural materials and man-made tools.” Visit these and other talented artists at the Montclair Village Art Walk which takes place on Mountain Boulevard at LaSalle Avenue. For more information, contact the Montclair Village Association at (510) 339-1000 or Pacific Fine Arts Festivals at (209) 267-4394, www. pacificfinearts.com. Presented by

articles.text: Police Sergeant David Cutler (middle) with his friends and family at a pinning ceremony on April 1. Piedmont Police Officer David Cutler was promoted to the rank of Sergeant in a pinning ceremony at the April 1 City Council meeting. In attendance were his wife Shannon and daughters Cassidy and Madison, as well as co-workers and members of his extended family. Cutler was honored for his promotion alongside Officer Jehan Liles, who was being recognized for his achievement in the department. In a speech to the city council, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers praised Cutler’s leadership in the department and congratulated him on the new role of being one of four sergeants in the department. “In addition to developing into a very dependable police officer over the years since I’ve been here, it’s been a pleasure watching you develop and grow and mature into the leader that you are today,” said Bowers. Cutler joined the police department in 2012 after a career in the Marine Corps. In his 12 years in Piedmont, Cutler has served as an acting watch commander, firearms instructor, police explorer advisor, and most recently as a police detective before his promotion. In addition to his law enforcement work, Cutler is also pursuing a master’s degree in criminal justice through an online program. “Oftentimes in policing, you get people who are one-trick ponies,” continued Bowers. “They’re either all tactics and high-speed stuff or community-oriented. David does both, which is so impressive to us.” When it came time to present the badge, Chief Bowers looked toward the other officers present with confusion. “Where’s the badge?” he asked. A beat followed. “Just kidding, April Fool’s,” he proclaimed, and the audience laughed. “I couldn’t help myself.” Cutler was pinned by recently retired Police Sergeant Robert Jaime, a mentor whose guidance Cutler said was instrumental in his career progression. “You know, you get a little emotional, but in a good way,” said Cutler. “To be pinned by someone who I respect greatly, to have it all come full circle is something I’ve worked really hard to achieve. And I didn’t do it alone.” In his new role, Cutler said he was most excited about the increased responsibility and opportunities for leadership. “I’m huge into leadership and giving back to those who have given to me. I’ve had some really good mentors throughout my career, and as a sergeant, it allows me to do that much more for the mentorships in my life.” Officer Cutler is pinned by his longtime mentor, retired PPD Sergeant Robert Jaime. pages.text: Wednesday, April 10, 2024 11 Police officer David Cutler promoted to Sergeant Police Sergeant David Cutler (middle) with his friends and family at a pinning ceremony on April 1. By Matt Simons Piedmont Police Officer David Cutler was promoted to the rank of Sergeant in a pinning ceremony at the April 1 City Council meeting. In attendance were his wife Shannon and daughters Cassidy and Madison, as well as co-workers and members of his extended family. Cutler was honored for his promotion alongside Officer Jehan Liles, who was being recognized for his achievement in the department. In a speech to the city council, Police Chief Jeremy Bowers praised Cutler’s leadership in the department and congratulated him on the new role of being one of four sergeants in the department. “In addition to developing into a very dependable police officer over the years since I’ve been here, it’s been a pleasure watching you develop and grow and mature into the leader that you are today,” said Bowers. Cutler joined the police department in 2012 after a career in the Marine Corps. In his 12 years in Piedmont, Cutler has served as an acting watch commander, firearms instructor, police explorer advisor, and most recently as a police detective before his promotion. In addition to his law enforcement work, Cutler is also pursuing a master’s degree in criminal justice through an online program. “Oftentimes in policing, you get people who are one-trick ponies,” continued Bowers. “They’re either all tactics and high-speed stuff or community-oriented. David does both, which is so impressive to us.” When it came time to present the badge, Chief Bowers looked toward the other officers present with confusion. “Where’s the badge?” he asked. A beat followed. “Just kidding, April Fool’s,” he proclaimed, and the audience laughed. “I couldn’t help myself.” Cutler was pinned by recently retired Police Sergeant Robert Jaime, a mentor whose guidance Cutler said was instrumental in his career progression. “You know, you get a little emotional, but in a good way,” said Cutler. “To be pinned by someone who I respect greatly, to have it all come full circle is something I’ve worked really hard to achieve. And I didn’t do it alone.” In his new role, Cutler said he was most excited about the increased responsibility and opportunities for leadership. “I’m huge into leadership and giving back to those who have given to me. I’ve had some really good mentors throughout my career, and as a sergeant, it allows me to do that much more for the mentorships in my life.” Officer Cutler is pinned by his longtime mentor, retired PPD Sergeant Robert Jaime. articles.text: Saturday, April 6 marked a monumental day for Piedmont High sophomore Layth Haddawy. He set four different state powerlifting records in the age 14-15 category at 132 pounds. At a U.S. Powerlifting Association meet in Oakland, he hit 280 pounds in the squat, 206 pounds on the bench press, a 371 pound dead lift, and the combined total record at 857 pounds. It’s a day Haddawy never expected when the school year started. He played on Piedmont’s JV football team in the fall and felt like he wasn’t making a big impact. But there was one place Haddawy always stood out with his peers – the weight room. “I began working out towards the end of 8th grade and into freshman year. Following the football season this year, I started looking into lifting and wound up meeting my coach. He said we’d need to train for a while before entering a meet,”Haddawy said. “I’ve been lifting for a while, but I began taking powerlifting very seriously in November when the football season ended. Throughout my life I’ve played all the team sports you can think of, but I never was great at any of them. I realized, especially in football, I wasn’t the best guy Layth Haddawy stands proudly after setting four California powerlifting records for age 14-15. on the field but I was always the strongest player on the team. I thought, if I’m too undersized for football, I should find something that fits me,” Haddawy said. Once the football season was over, Layth began training at Get Bent gym in Oakland under Layth Haddawy has qualified for the National Championships in powerlifting in Las Vegas in June. owner Jason Romero and coach James Cunningham. He began making big jumps over the following months. “When I first got there, my deadlift was about 310 and two months later, I was already around 360. I realized I had a lot of potential. My squat went from sub-200 to now around 280 pounds,” Haddawy described. The USPA 2024 Spring Break meet last weekend marked Haddawy’s first official competition. At the meet, lifters are allowed three reps to achieve their maximum weight and are permitted a fourth attempt if they are going for a State or National record. He eclipsed the one-year old squat record by 4.4 pounds, the two-year old bench record by 3.1 pounds, the one-year old deadlift record by 1.8 pounds, and the two-year old combined total record by 25 pounds. “I was really excited but nervous on the day of the meet. My coaches had me lower my attempts heavily to make sure I was nailing them and reaching my goals… On my third squat attempt, it warranted me taking a fourth try. It went well and I managed to break the State record for squat. Then came the bench, my second attempt was about eight points away from the State record. On the third attempt, I tweaked my form and I was able to do a slow, grind-it-out lift by about two points over the record.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team split its last two matches, defeating Western Alameda County Conference opponent Encinal in five sets in Alameda on Thursday, April 4 with scores of 26-24, 25-16, 16-25, 22-25, 15-11. They lost in five sets to non-league opponent Head-Royce the previous day. The loss to the Jayhawks came after the Highlanders won the opening two sets, but dropped the next three sets , 25-11, 25-18, 22-25, 25-27, 7-15 “I got cocky and switched up the lineup after the second set, I’m telling the team it’s my fault and it won’t happen again,” said a disappointed coach Mariah Cardenas. With a 5-6 league record, Piedmont must finish with an even .500 record to qualify for the North Coast Section playoffs. They’ll return from Spring Break to play five tough matches: Berkeley on April 15, Arroyo the next day, San Leandro on April 19, Castro Valley on April 23, and Bishop O’Dowd for the season-finale on April 26. The match with Head-Royce marked the debut season of Olivia Theut as the Jayhwks head coach. She graduated from Piedmont High in 2019. “There’s definitely a lot of pressure returning to your former high school. After the first game, we just talked about staying positive. It was such a competitive game and was a lot of fun to play against them,” Theut said. 3-2 loss to Head-Royce Piedmont dominated the first set with a 25-11 win, including five kills from John Champion, two from Spencer SorensenWald, and two by Mateo Devries. PHS also had a seven-point 25-18 win in the second set. There were five lead changes during the second set, but PHS took the lead at 18-17, leading to a 7-1 scoring run to close things with a 25-18 win. In an attempt by Cardenas to get players more time in different positions, the Jayhawks were able to storm back from then on. They John Champion had 19 kills against Head-Royce. articles.text: The exhibit Fashioning San Francisco: A Century of Style is now on view at the deYoung Museum in San Francisco. It features iconic collections of 20th and 21st-century women’s fashion in the United States and the Bay Area. The exhibition includes over 100 pieces, some loaned by local collectors of haute couture, and is the first major presentation of the museum’s own costume collection. A wide range of fashion is represented from French dressmakers to Japanese avant-garde designers. Designs by Christian Dior, Alexander McQueen, Christopher John Rogers, Comme des Garçons, Rei Kawakubo, Kei Ninomiya, Junya Watanabe, Yohji Yamamoto and Rodarte are on display. “These garments echo the evolving urban landscape of San Francisco, a city populated by structures that push the confines of modern architecture, likewise made by advanced engineering and with state-of-the-art industrial materials,” said Laura Camerlengo, curator of costume and textile arts at the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco.The exhibit is on display through August. Visit https://www. famsf.org/exhibitions/fashioning-san-francisco to learn more.

articles.text: Entries due Monday Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside’s annual haiku contest is currently underway. All entries are due by Monday, April 15. articles.text: The final Chamber Series concert of the season, Play on Words, will be performed at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Sunday, April 14, at 4 p.m. With former Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director René Mandel on violin, soprano Lisa Delan, cellist Evan Kahn, and pianist Kevin Korth, the audience will be taken on a literary journey from 19th-century Austria to the Golden Age of Hollywood to the present-day Bay Area. The Berkeley Symphony & Friends chamber music series, now in its 11th year, was founded by Mandel. Completed the year before his death, Franz Schubert’s monumental Piano Trio in E-flat Major, Op. 100 was among the last of his compositions he heard. It’s a dramatic work dappled with light: a Swedish folk song inspired the famous melody of the slow movement, which has appeared in films such as Barry Lyndon and The Piano Teacher. Erich Wolfgang Korngold’s Much Ado About Nothing Suite for Violin and Piano originated in 1918 as a commission of incidental music for the Shakespeare play. The young composer’s score made the production such a hit that the run was extended – but the orchestra’s musicians had already booked other gigs. Korngold thus created a more intimate arrangement, which has since become popular around the globe. Gordon Getty’s Four Dickinson Songs, which includes the arresting poem “Because I Could Not Stop for Death,” is a testament to the expressive power of Emily Dickinson. Getty has long admired Dickinson’s poetry: some of this music, for soprano and piano, dates back to his college days, and The White Election, another of his Dickinson cycles, comprises a staggering 32 songs. Jake Heggie’s Shed No Tear for soprano and piano evokes the natural world as illuminated by the poetry of John Keats: “Shed no tear! oh, shed no tear! The flower will bloom another year.” The music will be brought to life with soprano Lisa Delan and pianist Kevin Korth. Tickets are available at berkeleysymphony.org or by calling the Berkeley Symphony ticket office at (510) 841-2800. René Mandel, violin Soprano Lila Delan Kevin Korth, piano

articles.text: Berkeley Choro Ensemble will perform a concert with the great Douglas Lora at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, April 19 at 7:00 p.m. Tickets are $30 for General Admission and are available at https://www.bpt. me/6251519. Three-time Grammy nominee guitarist and composer Douglas Lora has established himself as one of the most prominent artists of his generation. He has collaborated with renowned artists YoYo Ma, Paquito d’Rivera, Assad Brothers, Anat Cohen, Marco Pereira, Jovino Santos Neto, Ney Rosauro, Marina Piccinini, and Paulo Bellinati. A member of the Brasil Guitar Duo, Trio Brasileiro and Caraivana, Lora has performed at major concert halls in the U.S., Europe, Asia and Latin America. He is the newest member of the awarded Los Angeles Guitar Quartet. His has taught at the University of Miami and Miami Conservatory of Music, and is the guitar instructor at Cal State Fullerton. The Berkeley Choro Ensemble is a group of world-class musicians from the SF Bay Area that debuted in 2010. The group celebrates the music, culture and history of Brazil, with a special Guitarist and composer Douglas Lora emphasis on the Choro genre, a style of music which emerged in the 1800s in Brazil, fusing the music of Brazil’s European immigrants and the native music of Brazil’s indigenous and African-Brazilian population. The choro sound is somewhat akin to a combination of European classical music, ragtime, and blues. Historically, the choro style influenced Brazil’s most famous classical composer, Heitor Villa Lobos, to compose some of the world’s most beautiful music, the Bachianas Brasileiras.

Escamillo is recast as a female dancer played by principal Dancer Jennifer Stahl and soloist Sasha Mukhamedov. The role of titular character Carmen is played by principal dancers Jasmine Jimison and Sasha De Sola. The ballet is accompanied by a score from Grammy Award–winning Arturo O’Farrill. Ochoa’s Broken Wings bring audiences into the world of celebrated Mexican painter Frida Kahlo. articles.text: Blue Door, Tanya Barfield’s new two-person play, premieres on the Aurora Theatre Company stage in Berkeley on Friday, April 19. Barf ield’s play features Lewis, a high-achieving Black mathematics professor, in conversation with three generations of his ancestors during a sleepless night as he wrestles with his own sense of self and cultural identity. Lewis is estranged from his white wife, who accuses him of being out of touch with his heritage for refusing to attend the Million Man March, a grassroots demonstration of African-American men in Washington, D.C., on October 16, 1995; organizers united in self-help and self-defense against economic and social ills plaguing their community. The ancestral visitations Lewis receives call upon joy and pain, as well as music and song to situate him in a long lineage of Black men in America from enslavement and Jim Crow to Black Power. Discussions of Blue Door will be held after the show on Friday, April 26; Tuesday, April 30; Friday, May 3; Wednesday, May 8; and Thursday, May 16. The play ends May 19. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.auroratheatre.org/index. php/shows-events/20232024-season/blue-door. Playwright Tanya Barfield

articles.text: World-renowned musical theater vocalist Patti LuPone performs at Davies Symphony Hall in San Francisco this Sunday, April 14. LuPone gained acclaim for her leading stage performances on Broadway and in London’s West End theater stage. She received three Laurence Olivier Awards, presented annually by the Society of London Theatre to recognize excellence in professional theater in London. In particular, for her performances as Fantine in the original London cast of Les Misérables, Moll in The Cradle Will Rock in 1985, and for Best Actress in a Supporting Role in a Musical for Company in 2019. LuPone is joined at Davies Symphony Hall by music director Joseph Thalken, director Scott Wittman and string instrumentalist Brad Phillips for a brandnew show she calls her “personal musical memoir.” The concert begins at 7:30 p.m. For more information and to purchase tickets, visit https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2023-24/Patti-LuPone. articles.text: A rousing celebration of Hispanic culture came off with the S.F. Ballet’s “Dos mujeres” program, continuing offstage well into the night before the large and wildly enthusiastic crowd. The entire Opera House was decorated high and low with multi-color South-of-the-Border images, including oversize flowers enhancing the box seats. The new Artistic Director Tamara Rojo hit the nail on the cabeza with her unique pairing, one celebrating the Mexican artist Frida Kahlo in the US-premiere gala spectacle Broken Wings, the other Carmen. Broken Wings is a glorious fantasy piece by Annabelle Lopez Ochoa, as if intended for the joyful Mexican Day of the Dead complete with amiable and ambulatory cadavers. If you were baffled by the gender mishmash, you were not alone. In the latter, dominant tall males with headdresses played female roles, much as in the Harvard Hasty Pudding comedy shows of old. And in Ariella Smith’s ballet, only distantly related to Carmen, the leading US-premiere of Lopez Ochoa’s Broken Wings at the San Francisco Ballet lady (Sasha de Sola on April 4) passionately kisses the bullfighter Escamillo, played by another woman (Jennifer Stahl). If the Smith Carmen had little to do with bullfights, gypsies, tabernas, the opera or Prosper Mérimée’s original novel, it allowed the tempestuous Carmen to ping-pong back and forth between a devoted father figure (Wei Wang) and the despised husband José in black (Joseph Walsh). It was as though the whole far-ranging drama of Carmen were transported to a spartan drawing room, with passions running wild, and Carmen literally sprinting all with them all over. A few measures of the Bizet opera are quoted in the opening of the helter-skelter Arturo O’Farrill’s score, which overall lacked the high drama required. But whatever Carmen lacked was made up for in the pageantry of Broken Wings, which deserves a rerun next season. This drama of the real-life Frida Kahlo wandering through the real world, a fantasy domain and ultimately a beautiful death was powered by the ballerina Isabella DeVivo, plucked from the ranks of mere soloists to take on Frida. On pointe, DeVivo appears to become airborne in scene after scene, unawed by the imaginary figures that encroach all about her. Playing a minor role as Frida’s (renowned) husband Diego was the robust guest artist from the Oregon Ballet Theatre, JohnPaul Simoens – a surprise loaner, given the raft of leading males in the 83-member S.F. Ballet roster who were untapped. No answer is forthcoming, so far. The wispy story line deals with Frida’s husband, her entering the underworld, then turning into a butterfly and fortified by a spirit headed heavenward. The music by Peter Salem included everything from the song-lament “La Llorona” to a mariachi bringing down the house. Overall, SFB director Rojo made her point several times over: These works were created by teams of women for the most part; and in this region we need some central, focal Latino cultural input, first on stage and extending to lavish Opera House Mexican décor. After the show comes a thunderous all-female mariachi (Mariachi Bonitas de Dinorah) in an unprecedented nightly lobby postlude. BALLET NOTES – Ochoa’s choreography had been featured here previously in her 2018 Guernica. Casts for this run change nightly. This program marked the company’s first-ever double bill of works by Latina choreographers. “DOS MUJERES” (Two Women), a program of Carmen and the US-premiere of Broken Wings, through April 14, by San Francisco Ballet. Opera House, S.F. For SFB info: (415) 865-2000, or go online www.sfballet.org.

articles.text: Remember the television program “The Twilight Zone”? If all goes well, you’ll be transported to Out of nowhere comes mysterious music. The narrator arrives on the set smoking a cigarette. “Good evening,“ he says. “Our story today is out of the ordinary. You might even call it a musical allegory. Our star is the guitar, an artistic masterpiece. Does any musical instrument have such sensual lines? Let’s just say that it has an inanimate sex appeal. Its history begins even before hisMusically, it appeals to every aspect of humanity. Does this sound like the Picture of Dorian Gray? It does. Let’s let Oscar Wilde tell the story of… The guitar in the twilight zone.” A huge crowd lines up to see an exhibition of the guitar. There are many on display, and the crowd expresses its admiration. Everyone wants to play it. The very first one is Noah’s grandfather. They say he invented the guitar. Leonardo da Vinci is next. Then come Bach and Vivaldi. They talk to each other a little bit and decide to write some guitar music. Not much time passes and Paganini sees his own guitar resting on plush velvet in all of its glory. He signs it with a flourish and gives it to his friend Berlioz who adds his signature. The crowd whispers: “It’s so beautiful.” Each, in turn, wants to try a tune. Andres Segovia wows the crowd with his playing. He uses a variety of foot stools. To change keys, he uses a capo. All of the classical guitarists copy this style of playing. But the unanimous decision is that the guitar needs more punch. They discover artificial amplification and loudspeakers. Problem solved! Guitar players from every country in the world discover that the guitar expresses world music. For convenience, they might use a pick and a neck strap. Someone comes up with the idea that the guitar needs a stronger tone. Let’s make an electric guitar, they decide. They do, and it becomes even more popular. The guitar adapts its personality to jazz, rock ‘n’ roll, heavy metal, yet remains as beautiful as ever. A few rock ‘n rollers find that smashing their guitars on stage is what they want to do. pages.text: Wednesday, April 10, 2024 19 The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The guitar in the twilight zone By Joseph Gold Remember the television program “The Twilight Zone”? If all goes well, you’ll be transported to another dimension. Out of nowhere comes mysterious music. The narrator arrives on the set smoking a cigarette. “Good evening,“ he says. “Our story today is out of the ordinary. You might even call it a musical allegory. Our star is the guitar, an artistic masterpiece. Does any musical instrument have such sensual lines? Let’s just say that it has an inanimate sex appeal. Its history begins even before history was recorded. Musically, it appeals to every aspect of humanity. Does this sound like the Picture of Dorian Gray? It does. Let’s let Oscar Wilde tell the story of… The guitar in the twilight zone.” A huge crowd lines up to see an exhibition of the guitar. There are many on display, and the crowd expresses its admiration. Everyone wants to play it. The very first one is Noah’s grandfather. They say he invented the guitar. Leonardo da Vinci is next. Then come Bach and Vivaldi. They talk to each other a little bit and decide to write some guitar music. Not much time passes and Paganini sees his own guitar resting on plush velvet in all of its glory. He signs it with a flourish and gives it to his friend Berlioz who adds his signature. The crowd whispers: “It’s so beautiful.” Each, in turn, wants to try a tune. Andres Segovia wows the crowd with his playing. He uses a variety of foot stools. To change keys, he uses a capo. All of the classical guitarists copy this style of playing. But the unanimous decision is that the guitar needs more punch. They discover artificial amplification and loudspeakers. Problem solved! Guitar players from every country in the world discover that the guitar expresses world music. For convenience, they might use a pick and a neck strap. Someone comes up with the idea that the guitar needs a stronger tone. Let’s make an electric guitar, they decide. They do, and it becomes even more popular. The guitar adapts its personality to jazz, rock ‘n’ roll, heavy metal, yet remains as beautiful as ever. A few rock ‘n rollers find that smashing their guitars on stage is what they want to do. People pay Classical guitarist Andres Segovia millions of dollars for an instrument, whether in good condition or smashed condition. The admiring crowd departs… not through the front entrance, but through the back door. Guitars on display in the museum are as beautiful as ever. But this is the twilight zone. There is always an allegory…a surprise knock-out punch. After all, Oscar Wilde wrote the screenplay. As the admiring crowd leaves the museum by the back door, they see a large pile of gear; footstools, capos, microphones and cables, amplification devices of all kinds, loud speakers and ear plugs, neck traps, tuners, slides, audio interface, looper pedals, ground lift, reverb devices, and costumes of all kind. On the very top is a smashed guitar. Wilde concludes his allegory with a group of lemmings playfully encircling the scene. The narrator returns to tell us he hopes we enjoyed the program. He smiles as he says: “Did you know that a group of lemmings is called a ‘suicide’?” Sic transit la gloria dei musica. (Thus is the glory of music.) articles.text: Thomas Hardy wrote Far From the Madding Crowd in 1874 during the height of the Victorian era. It was a time when women deferred to the wishes of men and were considered property to be acquired and then ignored. Men, in contrast, offered women safe harbor and financial security. Hardy’s story has proved timeless and prescient in great part because Hardy created in the character of Bathsheba Everdene ­ — an atypical woman who is independent, desiring to live on her own terms and not those dictated by a husband. She declares to a suitor that she wishes to be no man’s property. The film, starring Carey Mulligan as Bathsheba, is not only beautifully photographed, but Mulligan shines as she conveys the emotions of a woman who inherits a large farm and the title of mistress of all she surveys. She is determined to “astonish” all who now work for her and make a success of the farm, for she is no dilettante, but a woman who wishes to live on her own terms in a society where women are cloistered by custom and social mores. articles.text: Lightyear is a kid-friendly, action-adventure spin-off from Disney-Pixar’s Toy Story. Parents might consider the following: if your little guys have not been introduced to the Toy Story franchise, well, begin there before heading on to Lightyear. Here is some backstory: in 1995, the year that the first Toy Story was released, it began with Andy, a boy who had a bevy of plastic toy-figures in his room. Buzz Lightyear was not one of them. What happened was that Andy went to the movies and watched a sci-fi action adventure film starring Buzz Lightyear, and he was smitten. He loved the character, which became an action figure. For Christmas, of course, under the tree was Buzz Lightyear. What Lightyear is not is a film about how Buzz ends up in Andy’s room, joining the gang of figures that come to life, so to speak. Instead, Lightyear is the film that captured Andy’s imagination. In other words, it’s sort of an origin tale that stands alone and is only referenced in Toy Story. So far so good? The question then begged is, “what was there about this animated story that so captured Andy’s imagination?” First, the tale unfolds with Buzz (Chris Evans), a charismatic, all-American, lantern-jawed space ranger and a crew of hundreds on board A scene from Disney-Pixar’s Lightyear a Star Trek-like deep space star ship, akin to the iconic Enterprise. In command is Alisha Hawthorne (Uzo Aduba). The ship is 4.2 million light years from Earth on a deep space mission; all have been in deep hibernation. Awakened, they decide to explore an unfamiliar planet named T’Kani Prime. Of course, stuff happens that provides excitement. The planet has breathable air; however, the ship is damaged on landing. Plus, there are hostile, voracious insect-like creatures that threaten the crew. What allows the ship to travel at warp speed is a hyperspeed crystal that is also in need of repair. Of course, Buzz is the obvious choice to be the test pilot. This is when time travel comes into play and the story does get a bit convoluted. Buzz takes the crystal out for a very short test; however, when he returns he discovers that four years have passed on the planet. There’s also an evil emperor, Zurg (James Brolin), who threatens the new colony now established on T’Kani Prime. He has an army of robotic soldiers. There is also a scene-stealing robotic cat named Sox (voiced by Pixar director Peter Sohn) who is Buzz’s close companion. Think of the critter as Buzz’s feline wingman and advisor. It’s all wonderfully animated, filled with lots of action and adventure, and a great introduction to Buzz Lightyear — a swaggering daredevil, dedicated to the mission no matter the breathtaking risk. Lightyear. Directed by Angus MacLane. Disney-Pixar animation. Voiced by Chris Evans, Taika Waititi, Keke Palmer. Rated PG. 1 hr., 40 min. Released in 2022.

Be careful when naming beneficiaries You might not have thought much about beneficiary designations, but they can play a big role in your estate planning. When you purchase insurance policies and open investment accounts, such as your IRA, you’ll be asked to name a beneficiary, and, in some cases, more than one. This might seem easy, especially if you have a spouse and children, but if you experience a major life event, such as a divorce or a death in the family, you may need to make some changes because beneficiary designations carry a lot of weight under the law. In fact, these designations can supersede the instructions you may have written in your will or living trust, so everyone in your family should know who is expected to get which assets. One significant benefit of having proper beneficiary designations in place is that they may enable beneficiaries to avoid the time-consuming — and possibly expensive — probate process. The beneficiary issue can become complex because not everyone reacts the same way to events such as divorce — some people want their ex-spouses to still receive assets while others don’t. Furthermore, not all the states have the same rules about how beneficiary designations are treated after a divorce. And some financial assets are treated differently than others. Here’s the big picture: If you’ve named your spouse as a beneficiary of an IRA, bank or brokerage account, insurance policy, will or trust, this beneficiary designation will automatically be revoked upon divorce in about half the states. So, if you still want your ex-spouse to get these assets, you will need to name them as a non-spouse beneficiary after the divorce. But if you’ve named your spouse as beneficiary for a 401(k) plan or pension, the designation will remain intact until and unless you change it, regardless of where you live. However, in community property states, couples are generally required to split equally all assets they acquired during their marriage. When couples divorce, the community property laws require they split their assets 50/50, but only those assets they obtained while they lived in that state. If you were to stay in the same community property state throughout your marriage and divorce, the ownership issue is generally straightforward, but if you were to move to or from one of these states, it might change the joint ownership picture. Thus far, we’ve only talked about beneficiary designation issues surrounding divorce. But if an ex-spouse — or any beneficiary — passes away, the assets will generally pass to a contingent beneficiary — which is why it’s important that you name one at the same time you designate the primary beneficiary. Also, it may be appropriate to name a special needs trust as beneficiary for a family member who has special needs or becomes disabled. If this individual were to be the direct beneficiary, any assets passing directly into their hands could affect their eligibility for certain programs. You may need to work with a legal professional to sort out beneficiary designation issues and the rules that apply in your state. But you may also want to do a beneficiary review with your financial advisor whenever you experience a major life event, such as a marriage, divorce or the addition of a new child. Your investments, retirement accounts and life insurance proceeds are valuable assets — and you want them to go where you intended. articles.text: Twenty-one members of the First Monday Reading group met at the Japanese Tea House. In Piedmont Park on April 1 to discuss Maya Angelou’s 1969 autobiography, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings. The book was on The New York Times paperback bestseller list for two years. It has been required reading in some schools, including Piedmont High. However the book’s depiction of childhood rape, racism, and sexuality has caused it to be banned in other schools and libraries. articles.text: While I was tending to my new hydrangea patch last week, a passerby stopped to remark upon my garden. “I walk past your yard every day,” he said, “and I’m always impressed at how cottagecore it is.” “Thanks,” I said, not exactly sure if this was a compliment. (Turns out it’s an Instagram hashtag referencing dreamy pastoral scenes.) Pointing past my split-rail fence to the massive clusters of purple flowers rising out of the broad-leaved foliage along the creek, the young man asked. “What are those?” I get this question a lot this time of year. Even in the showiest of gardens these flowers stand out. But nobody ever believes me when I tell them that they are geraniums. The geraniums that you probably have in mind – the sun loving, (usually) red ones with slightly fuzzy leaves, the ones growing out of Parisian planter boxes in oil paintings – are not actually geraniums. At least, not anymore. When so-called geraniums were introduced to the gardening public back in the 1700s, they had been categorized into an eponymous genus by Carl Linneaus, the father of modern taxonomy. Some 80 years later, however, a French botanist reclassified that group of species into a different genus, Pelargonium. Botanists accepted the change, but the gardening public didn’t—so “geranium” is what the common man has been calling these plants ever since. My geraniums are, in fact, the real deal. Which is a funny thing to say given that they look and act like something out of science fiction. The Geramium maderense, as it’s known, grows three to four feet tall and wide and puts out dinner-plate sized, jagged-edged leaves that seem almost tropical. It blooms in the second year by pushing up an enormous bouquet Geramium maderense in bloom in early spring Photo by Josh Harskinson of flowers from a central stalk. And then it dies. You won’t mind, however. They prolifically reseed themselves. I think I started with two or three plants and this year I must have at least 30. While most geraniums hail from the Mediterranean region, these unique plants are endemic to the island of Madeira, a Portuguese territory located in the Atlantic Ocean some 280 nautical miles from the coast of North Africa. It has a foggy and temperate climate like that of San Francisco and was once covered with a forest of evergreen laurel trees. The Geranium maderense grows in the understory, though it is now seldom seen in the wild. In the Bay Area, you can see Madeira geraniums growing in Golden Gate Park near the Queen Wilhemina garden. I have planted mine on a slope beneath oak trees. They require little sunlight and can survive through the summer with minimal water. They prefer acidic soil of the sort that comes naturally from abundant tree leaf litter. Give them plenty of space – this is not a planter box geranium! The older leaves will bend towards the ground to become supports for the plant before it pushes up its flower stalk. Trust me, the spectacular blooms are worth the two-year wait. Journalist and ardent gardener Josh Harkinson lives along a creek near Piedmont Avenue with two kids, four chickens, and a wife who thinks he spends too much time gardening. Suddenly, this 19th century woman begins to lose her moorings and is confronted with a series of choices that most women of this period could never have imagined. But her vulnerability stems from a confused heart, not from a lack of financial independence. How Bathsheba sorts out this existential moment makes for a genuinely fine narrative, delivered by an excellent cast. As a period film, Far From the Madding Crowd is compelling and solidly engaging. Tangentially, the Brits adapted Hardy’s novel in 1967. Directed by John Schlesinger, the film starred Julie Christie, Alan Bates, Peter Finch and Terence Stamp. At the time, it was considered a tour de force. Christie’s startling beauty gave the film a far different look than this recent incarnation. Mulligan is in many ways a more interesting casting choice, her independence and allure drawn from her convictions and not overshadowed by her appearance. Far From the Madding Crowd. articles.text: Piedmont Food Fest 3 is coming to town in two weeks and the organizers are eager to unveil a completely reimagined community experience that’s been in the works for six months. Building on the success of the first two years, the Piedmont Food Fest team has re-examined every dimension of the festival to find new ways to inspire and delight attendees. Since its premiere in April 2022 and return last year, Piedmont Food Fest has attracted over 3000 attendees who’ve enjoyed the mix of multicultural food, drink, and performances curated from all around the Bay Area. From quesabirrias to pork belly buns to hot chicken sandwiches, from boba milk tea to gourmet lemonade, Food Festers have grown accustomed to discovering something delicious and new at this newest Piedmont tradition. This year, organizers will turn Magnolia Avenue into a veritable food boulevard helping hungry attendees easily stroll by the many options, making it easy to go back for seconds and even thirds. The Food Zone will feature 22 food vendors, including new additions Tea on Piedmont, Lola’s Spanish Cuisine, Doc Bones BBQ as well as the Nepalese food truck Momolicious of recent Steph Curry-inspired internet fame. Food Festers will also discover the Sweet Zone, located by the Community Circle, where they can indulge in handmade gelato from Hila, Japanese crepes from BB Tea Station, banana bread pudding from OG Desserts, Taiwanese pineapple cakes from Annie’s T Cakes while getting to know local non-profits, retailers, and community groups such as Oakland Roots, Soccer Without Borders, No Immigrants No Spice, Piedmont Language School, and Immedium Books. Food Festers are advised to come early to get a good seat and enjoy this year’s performances, which include the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, Oakland Taiko, Beloved Little Circus, O Hina’aro Nui Tahitian Dance & Music, Hiiiwav Black Artist Incubator, Devendra Sharma Folk Opera Ensemble, and Amor do Samba. No Immigrants No Spice will be bringing back their interactive trivia game and audience members will hear from Chef James Yeun Leong Parry from Michelin-rated restaurant Benu and most recently his Chinese pop-up, The Happy Crane. For more information see: www. piedmontfoodfest.org.

Building on the success of the first two years, the Piedmont Food Fest team has re-examined every dimension of the festival to find new ways to inspire and delight attendees. Since its premiere in April 2022 and return last year, Piedmont Food Fest has attracted over 3000 attendees who’ve enjoyed the mix of multicultural food, drink, and performances curated from all around the Bay Area. From quesabirrias to pork belly buns to hot chicken sandwiches, from boba milk tea to gourmet lemonade, Food Festers have grown accustomed to discovering something delicious and new at this newest Piedmont tradition. This year, organizers will turn Magnolia Avenue into a veritable food boulevard helping hungry attendees easily stroll by the many options, making it easy to go back for seconds and even thirds. The Food Zone will feature 22 food vendors, including new additions Tea on Piedmont, Lola’s Spanish Cuisine, Doc Bones BBQ as well as the Nepalese food truck Momolicious of recent Steph Curry-inspired internet fame. Food Festers will also discover the Sweet Zone, located by the Community Circle, where they can indulge in handmade gelato from Hila, Japanese crepes from BB Tea Station, banana bread pudding from OG Desserts, Taiwanese pineapple cakes from Annie’s T Cakes while getting to know local non-profits, retailers, and community groups such as Oakland Roots, Soccer Without Borders, No Immigrants No Spice, Piedmont Language School, and Immedium Books. Food Festers are advised to come early to get a good seat and enjoy this year’s performances, which include the Great Wall Youth Orchestra, Oakland Taiko, Beloved Little Circus, O Hina’aro Nui Tahitian Dance & Music, Hiiiwav Black Artist Incubator, Devendra Sharma Folk Opera Ensemble, and Amor do Samba. No Immigrants No Spice will be bringing back their interactive trivia game and audience members will hear from Chef James Yeun Leong Parry from Michelin-rated restaurant Benu and most recently his Chinese pop-up, The Happy Crane. For more information see: www. piedmontfoodfest.org.
